extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants/attorneys in AMS (ASEAN Member States)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination and drafting of patent claims and specifications focusing on clarity, permissible claim types/phrasing, support by the description, and sufficiency of disclosure (enablement/best mode) in AMS. Covers claim formats, prohibited/acceptable terms, drawings, dependencies, product-by-process, ranges, disclaimers, and experimental sufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition phrases and claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: In evaluating novelty or inventive step, the examiner should consider which type of transition phrase, such as “consisting of,” “comprising,” “characterized by,” or “consisting essentially of” is used in the claims. The subject matter to be searched depends on the type of transition phrase used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT ISPE GL §5.20-5.23 apply mutatis mutandis; treat “comprising” as open-ended and “consisting of” as closed-ended; choice of transitional phrase affects the boundaries of the claimed subject-matter and search scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims expressed as means-plus-function should be treated according to established PCT guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT ISPE GL §5.25 apply mutatis mutandis (i.e., apply PCT guidance for interpretation and support of means-plus-function claim elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim defines a product in terms of the process by which the product is made, the claim as a whole is directed to a product. Such a claim lacks novelty if a prior art product, even if made by an undisclosed process, is inherently the same as the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a product can only be defined by process steps, examiner should consider the process steps in search and patentability assessment; example provided (two-layer welded panel) where welding imparts distinctive properties — process informs novelty/inventive step analysis; see Chapter appendix for more guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and apparatus limitations in process claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim relates to a process for producing the product of the invention, the process as claimed should, when carried out reasonably by a PSIA, necessarily result in that particular product; otherwise there is internal inconsistency and lack of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should ensure the process steps as claimed lead to the claimed product; internal inconsistencies between product and process features render claims unclear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistency between claims and description
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be consistent with the description; amendments to claims should be supported by and consistent with the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT ISPE GL §5.29-5.30 apply mutatis mutandis; if claim amendments are made to meet clarity, corresponding description amendments may be required; avoid inconsistency that broadens claim scope beyond description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement — meaning clear to PSIA from claim wording alone
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of the terms of a claim must be clear for a Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA) from the wording of the claim alone. Clarity must be analysed in light of the application disclosure, prior art teachings, and PSIA interpretation at the time the invention was made; if a PSIA can determine claim boundaries with reasonable certainty, the claim complies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breadth is not equivalent to lack of clarity; examiner considers disclosure and context; references to PCT ISPE GL paragraphs on clarity (5.32-5.33).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claim must specify essential features
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention, except insofar as such features are implied by generic terms used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim to a “bicycle” need not mention wheels; ensure essential features are present or clearly implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity applies to individual claims and the claim set as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement that the claims should be clear applies both to individual claims and to the set of claims as a whole, irrespective of product, process or product-by-process claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine both singular claims and how claims interact; ensure no internal contradictions across claim set (PCT ISPE GL references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims defining products by reference to other products/use relationships require precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim for an apparatus or a product seeks to define the invention by reference to features of the use to which the apparatus or product is put, lack of clarity can result (especially when defining by relationship to a second product not part of the claimed invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May need to reword (e.g., use “connectable” instead of “connected”), or claim the combination (e.g., “engine with a cylinder head”); permissibility of defining dimensions/shape of first product by reference to second product allowed in some cases (example: number-plate bracket).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms not allowed (indefinite/relative/ambiguous/approximation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain words may be regarded as ambiguous, inadequate, unclear, or too broad (e.g., “thin”, “wide”, “strong”, terms of approximation like “about”, “approximately”, ambiguous expressions like “preferably”, “more preferably”, “in particular”, “substantially”, “mostly”, “similarly”, “for example”, “such as”, adverbs, references like “as described in part…”, trademarks, and multi-outcome expressions like “and/or”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term of degree appears, examiner should determine whether PSIA would be apprised of its meaning via disclosure of measurement standards in the description or from prior art; expressions of the type “preferably”, “for example” are generally regarded as non-limiting (i.e., feature following is optional); invite applicant to define or excise unclear terms where possible without adding new subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imprecise terms — case-by-case assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that includes vague or equivocal wording which leaves reader in doubt as to scope should be objected to for lack of clarity. Terms like “substantially”, “about”, “more or less”, “approximately” may be objectionable depending on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether such terms prevent unambiguous distinction from prior art; raise novelty/inventive-step objections if ‘about’ prevents clear distinction; ‘comprising’ allowed as open-ended, ‘consisting of’ closed-ended, ‘characterised by’ allowed in two-part claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-to-be-achieved claims — allowed if verifiable and achievable
rubrics_metrics.description: No objection should be raised if the invention can only be defined by a result-to-be-achieved, provided the result is achievable without undue experimentation and can be directly and positively verified by tests or procedures adequately specified in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must specify tests/procedures in the description; verifier must be reproducible and not rely on trial-and-error beyond routine methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of product or process by parameters — allowed if objectively determinable
rubrics_metrics.description: A product may be defined by parameters (e.g., chemical/physical parameters) where the invention cannot be adequately defined otherwise, provided parameters can be clearly and reliably determined by indications in the description or by objective procedures recognised in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameters not recognised in the art or requiring non-accessible apparatus for measurement may be objectionable; examiners should watch for applicants using unusual parameters to disguise lack of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers and negative limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter of a claim may be limited by disclaimers, negative limitations, or exclusions (e.g., “free of water”). Negative limitations are not per se ambiguous if each recited limitation is clear; negative limitation is unclear if it attempts to claim by excluding what was not invented rather than reciting what was invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative limitations can be used to meet novelty; examples given where exclusions are clear; ensure negative limitation's boundaries are definite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and multiplicity of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be objected to as lacking conciseness when they are unduly multiplied or duplicative; the number of claims must be considered relative to the nature of the invention the applicant seeks to protect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT ISPE GL §5.42 apply mutatis mutandis; examiner may object to excessive/duplicative claims; consider practicality and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives within a claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may refer to alternatives, provided the number and presentation of alternatives in a single claim does not make the claim obscure or difficult to construe and provided the claim meets unity requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how alternatives are presented; excessive or poorly presented alternatives may render claim obscure; ensure unity is satisfied (EPO GL reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for drawings and figures in relation to clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: If drawings are included, they should first be briefly described (e.g., “Figure 1 is a plan view...”); when referring to drawing elements in the description, refer to the element name as well as its number; description and drawings should be consistent (reference numbers and signs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AMS-specific regulations for drawings; avoid ambiguous references like “3 is connected to 5 via 4” — prefer “resistor 3 is connected to capacitor 5 via switch 4”; ensure consistency of reference numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims — format and allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependency of claims is allowed; multiple dependent claims (referring to more than one other claim) are allowed in the AMS. A multiple dependent claim includes all limitations contained in the claim(s) to which it relates. Dependent claims should be grouped together practically to enable association.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent office may follow alternative guidelines: (a) multiple dependent claim referring to more than one claim should do so only alternatively and cannot form a basis for other multiple dependent claims; or (b) may allow alternative or cumulative references and allow multiple dependent claims to form basis for other multiple dependent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-part, two-part claims and two-part form
rubrics_metrics.description: Many AMS prefer the two-part form where the claim is sectioned into pre-characterising (state of the art/prior-art features) and characterising (inventive features) parts, separated by transitional phrase like “characterised in that” or “characterised by.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First part should indicate designation (technical class) and necessary prior-art features relevant to the invention; second part states the technical features that add to prior art; two-part form unnecessary or unsuitable if it distorts invention or prior art; example regarding camera vs shutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of independent claims and unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Most AMS do not limit the number of independent claims in an application. Several independent claims in the same category directed to interrelated subject-matter may meet unity even if the claimed subject-matter appears quite different, provided technical features making a contribution over the prior art are the same or corresponding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider unity and technical contribution when multiple independent claims are present; references to EPO guidance on number of independent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims — equivalence to process claims for examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Use claims are allowed in most AMS (with specified country exceptions); for examination, a use claim in form “the use of substance X as an insecticide” is regarded as equivalent to a process claim “a process of killing insects using substance X.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interpret such a use claim as directed to the substance per se as an amplifying circuit or to building processes; note country-specific exceptions (e.g., Lao PDR and Viet Nam, Indonesia limited to new products).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ranges (e.g., dosage) in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of ranges in claims is explicitly allowed in some AMS under prescribed conditions. A specific example in the prior art that falls within a claimed range anticipates the range claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art discloses a range that overlaps the claimed narrow range, novelty must be decided case-by-case; narrow selection ranges may still be novel/inventive if evidence (e.g., unexpected results) shows selection produces effects within that narrow range; see Chapter 11 for inventive step considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of limitations and disclaimers in claims (reprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter of a claim may be limited by disclaimers or negative limitations to meet novelty; negative limitation is acceptable where each recited limitation is clear; mere absence of a positive recitation is not a basis for exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative limitations should not be used to try to claim by excluding what applicant did not invent; ensure clarity of each excluded element; examples included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of claims allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Product, process and product-by-process claims are allowed in all AMS; use claims are allowed in most AMS. Most AMS prefer certain claim formats (e.g., two-part form). Independent claims directed to essential features, followed by reasonable dependent claims, are permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two basic kinds: product (physical entity) and activity (process/use). Include reasonable number of dependent claims even if their features might constitute inventions on their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be supported by the description and drawings (support requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims (independent and dependent) must be fully supported by the description; there must be a basis in the description for the subject-matter of every claim and the claims' scope may not be broader than justified by the description and drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is regarded as supported unless PSIA would be unable to extend teaching to whole claimed field using routine methods; vague statements or assertions without technical content do not provide basis; raise objection of lack of support only if well-founded and, where possible, supported by published documents; treat clarity/support separate from novelty/inventive step/industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of claim must be supported by description when made to meet clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment of a claim should be supported by the description and be clear and concise to meet clarity requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims are amended for clarity, ensure description is amended as necessary (PCT ISPE GL §5.29). Avoid introducing added subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure (enablement) — general requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application is sufficiently disclosed if it provides enough details to enable a PSIA to 'carry out the invention'. All AMS require a specification that sufficiently discloses the invention; some AMS additionally require disclosure of the 'best mode'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description (with drawings if any) must give a detailed description of at least one way of carrying out the invention; disclosure should enable PSIA to make and use the invention and to understand the technical problem and solution; well-known ancillary features need not be detailed, but any feature essential for carrying out the invention must be described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant responsibility and remedies for insufficient disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficiency of disclosure is the applicant's responsibility; if examiner considers disclosure insufficient, the deficiency cannot be cured after filing by adding new examples or features that introduce subject-matter beyond the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insufficient disclosure could be remedied by restricting claims to embodiments sufficiently described and deleting other embodiments; objections presuppose serious doubts substantiated by verifiable facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider for undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether undue experimentation is required to carry out the claimed invention, consider: (i) breadth of the claims; (ii) nature of the invention; (iii) general knowledge of a PSIA; (iv) level of predictability in the art; (v) amount of direction provided in the application (including references to prior art); and (vi) amount of experimentation required to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See PCT ISPE 5.48–5.51 for more details; use these factors to decide whether disclosure enables PSIA without undue experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable insufficiency examples — chance-dependent and physically impossible inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two instances where insufficiency is essentially irreparable: (a) successful performance depends on chance (results not reproducible or success totally unreliable), and (b) successful performance is inherently impossible because it would be contrary to well-established physical laws (e.g., perpetual motion machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish chance-dependent irreproducibility from acceptable production processes that have some failures if satisfactory parts can be sorted non-destructively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof regarding sufficiency of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, the burden of proof on sufficiency lies with the party raising the objection. If there are serious doubts about the possibility of performing the invention, the burden of proof or a demonstration that success is credible rests with the applicant or patent proprietor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When serious doubts exist, request evidence from applicant/proprietor to show reproducibility or credibility of success (applicant must demonstrate performance credibly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement in some AMS
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AMS (Cambodia, Malaysia, Myanmar, Thailand) require applicants to disclose the 'best mode' of carrying out the invention in addition to enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where best mode is required, the specification must set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor at filing; ensure compliance with jurisdiction-specific requirements.
